what_space_cost_includes: CLPS order to carry and operate PRIME-1 on the lunar surface (IM-2)
what_earth_cost_includes: Honeybee contract: manufacturing and Earth testing of the flight drill
notes: The delivery to the Moon alone cost ~6.6 times as much as building and testing the drill on Earth. With Spaceflight Now's 62.5 M figure the ratio would be 8.2. The lunar demo was not completed (lander tipped over).

what_space_cost_includes: Development of the Pathfinder lander/EDL, whose goal was to demonstrate low-cost landing on Mars (without launcher or operations)
what_earth_cost_includes: ILC Dover airbag system (hardware; tested in ~20 drops with prototypes and in the Plum Brook vacuum chamber)
pair_type: proxy (the Earth cost is the airbag hardware, not the stand-alone test campaign)
notes: The stand-alone cost of the Plum Brook drop tests was not found. The ratio compares the full demo on Mars with the airbag subsystem.

what_earth_cost_includes: One-year budget line (2018) to develop and test the helicopter, including tests in JPL's 25-foot space simulator
notes: The 23 M was taken from a Wikipedia excerpt, not from an opened page. The 85 M already includes the Earth tests, so the ratio is biased downward. The cost of the chamber campaign is not published.

what_space_cost_includes: MOXIE instrument aboard Perseverance (approximate figure from the principal investigator)
what_earth_cost_includes: SBIR Phase II to OxEon (maker of the MOXIE cells): long-duration Earth test of SOXE stacks (5,000-10,000 h) and test bench
pair_type: proxy (successor technology, not the same instrument)
notes: On Mars, MOXIE ran for 1,213 minutes over 16 cycles; the Earth contract plans 5,000-10,000 hours of testing. The SBIR figure comes from a search excerpt.

what_space_cost_includes: HYPOTHETICAL ESTIMATE: delivery of 100 kg (ASSUMED mass, not published) at 1.2 M USD/kg at Astrobotic's rate
what_earth_cost_includes: Average per company of the 19.4 M USD contract to build 3 prototypes and run environmental tests (thermal vacuum in JSC Chamber A, 2024)
notes: VSAT has not flown yet. Additional one-off test: 1.1 M USD (Astrobotic SBIR Phase III, 'VSAT and LunaRay testing', 2026, https://www.federalcompass.com/fed-contract-award/80NSSC26C0010). The liquid nitrogen for Chamber A alone runs about 10,560 USD/day (2012 figure, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20130011554/downloads/20130011554.pdf).

what_space_cost_includes: ESTIMATE: 2 kg × 1.2 M USD/kg (Astrobotic's public rate); the actual price of Iris's trip is not public
what_earth_cost_includes: Total project cost of the rover (construction and Earth testing, CMU students)
notes: The ticket to the Moon alone would cost about 3 times the entire, already tested rover. Peregrine failed and Iris never reached the surface.

artifact: 1 kg of payload: a week on the Moon vs. a week in a NASA vacuum chamber (JSC ESTA)
what_space_cost_includes: 1 kg delivered to the lunar surface at Astrobotic's rate (includes ~192 h of surface operation)
what_earth_cost_includes: ESTIMATE: one 1-week (5-day) test in JSC's 20-foot vacuum chamber = fiscal year 2025 payments (292,478.91 USD) ÷ 5 tests per year at most
pair_type: generic proxy (per kg vs. per test)
notes: The Sandia agreement totals 1,189,812.61 USD for up to 5 tests/year over ~3.5 years. If fewer tests are run, each one costs more. With 10 kg the ratio would be ~205×.
